items.title: UK GDPR, Article 15: Right of access by the data subject
items.locator: Art. 15(1)(h), 15(1A) and 15(3); textual amendment notes F4, F5 and F8
items.quote: based on a reasonable and proportionate search for the personal data and other information described in that paragraph
items.why: The access right. Paragraph 1A limits it to what a reasonable and proportionate search can provide; inserted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 s.78(1)(a), in force at Royal Assent (s.142(2)(b)) and treated as in force from 1 January 2024 (s.78(5)). Point (h) requires meaningful information about the logic of automated decisions that are subject to the Article 22C safeguards. Year is the year of the latest amendment shown.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 17: Right to erasure ('right to be forgotten')
items.quote: the controller shall have the obligation to erase personal data without undue delay where one of the following grounds applies
items.why: The erasure duty and its limits: it applies only on the listed grounds (for example data no longer necessary, consent withdrawn, a successful objection, unlawful processing) and not where paragraph 3 applies. Nothing in the article excludes data held in AI systems. Read with Article 19 (telling recipients) and Article 11 (where the person cannot be identified).

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 21: Right to object
items.quote: The controller shall no longer process the personal data unless the controller demonstrates compelling legitimate grounds for the processing
items.why: The objection right, expressly including profiling. It applies only where the lawful basis is Article 6(1)(e), (ea) or (f), and the controller may continue on compelling legitimate grounds; the objection to direct marketing in paragraphs 2 and 3 has no such exception. '(ea)' added 5 February 2026 by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 s.70(5).

items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: How do we ensure individual rights in our AI systems?
items.locator: Sections 'How should we ensure individual rights requests for training data?', 'How should we ensure individual rights requests for AI outputs?' and 'How do individual rights relate to data contained in the model itself?'
items.quote: When procuring an AI service, you must choose one which allows individual rights to be protected and enabled
items.why: Source of the brief's quotation (training data section). Rights apply to training data, to inputs and outputs in deployment, and to data contained in a model. Requests are not manifestly unfounded or excessive just because AI makes them harder; erasing training data does not mean erasing the model unless the model contains the data or can be used to infer it; rectification or erasure inside a model may need re-training or deletion. Under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. Year not shown on the page; follows earlier reading lists, to confirm.

items.title: Response to the consultation series on generative AI: Engineering individual rights into generative AI models
items.locator: Section 'Our response'; also 'In brief' and 'Key points from the responses'
items.quote: these may not be sufficient, as they do not actually remove the data from the model
items.why: The regulator's stated position, not statutory guidance: organisations must have mechanisms to fulfil requests for training data and, if a model contains personal data, for the model itself; output filters may not be enough; Article 11 must not be used to avoid obligations; no clear evidence was received of practical measures, and machine unlearning was argued mainly in theory. The page shows no publication date, so the year is the year it was read; it refers to the Data (Use and Access) Bill, so it predates the 2025 Act.

items.title: Right of access: How do we find and retrieve the relevant information?
items.locator: Sections 'What efforts do we need to make to find information?', 'What about archived information and backup records?' and 'What about personal information in big datasets?'
items.quote: However, there is no technology exemption from the right of access.
items.why: How far a search must go after the 2025 Act: reasonable and proportionate, and the organisation must be able to show why a search would not be. Observed and inferred information about a person is within the right. Expects adequate metadata and the ability to query for everything held about one person. Date is the 'latest updates' date shown on the page. The companion page on preparing for requests recommends information asset registers and a request log.

items.title: Data protection audit framework, artificial intelligence toolkit: Contracts and third parties
items.locator: List beginning 'Include terms or clauses stating that'
items.quote: the processor must take appropriate measures to help the controller respond to requests from people to exercise their rights
items.why: What the regulator's auditors look for in AI supplier contracts; the underlying duty is UK GDPR Article 28(3)(e). The toolkit has no separate section on individual rights. 'Under review' banner following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; the page shows no publication date, so the year is the year it was read.

items.title: Opinion 28/2024 on certain data protection aspects related to the processing of personal data in the context of AI models
items.locator: Para. 43 (p. 16); also para. 65 (p. 21) and the lists of mitigating measures on pp. 29-30 and para. 114 (p. 32)
items.quote: By default, SAs should consider that AI models are likely to require a thorough evaluation of the likelihood of identification
items.why: EU comparator on whether a trained model still holds personal data, which decides whether rights reach the model. A model is anonymous only if the likelihood of extracting personal data, directly or through queries, is insignificant. Lists unlearning and erasure beyond the legal minimum as mitigating measures, and notes that regulators may order erasure of a dataset or a model. Not binding in the UK.

items.title: 2025 Coordinated Enforcement Action: Implementation of the right to erasure by controllers
items.quote: a total of 764 controllers responded to the questionnaire
items.why: Source of the figure. Seven recurring issues, the first being 'Absence of a documented and updated internal procedure to handle erasure requests'; others include erasure in back-ups and weak anonymisation used in place of deletion. Covers erasure generally, not AI, and the European Economic Area, not the UK. The PDF gives the adoption date as 10 February 2026.

items.title: Machine Unlearning Doesn't Do What You Think: Lessons for Generative AI Policy and Research
items.quote: unlearning is not a general-purpose solution for circumscribing generative-AI model behavior in service of broader positive impact
items.why: Research support for caution about promising to remove one person's data from a trained model: the authors identify mismatches between what unlearning aims at and what can be implemented. Abstract only read in this pass; version 2 dated 31 October 2025.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 12A: Meaning of "applicable time period"
items.locator: Art. 12A(1)-(4); note F1; read with Art. 12(3)-(4)
items.quote: the period of one month beginning with the relevant time
items.why: The statutory clock the criterion's 'within statutory timescales' refers to, missing from this list. One month from the latest of receipt of the request, of any identity information asked for, or of any fee; extendable by two further months for complex or numerous requests, by notice given within the first month with reasons. Inserted on 5 February 2026 by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 s.76(3) (note F1; S.I. 2026/82); no outstanding effects shown. The address ends in a full stop; without it the site returns 'page not found'. Year is the year of the latest amendment shown.

items.title: Data Protection Act 2018, section 164A: Complaints by data subjects to controllers
items.quote: A controller must facilitate the making of complaints under this section
items.why: A new duty that bears directly on rights readiness and is not in the brief. Anyone who thinks their data has been mishandled may complain to the organisation, which must make complaining easy (for example an electronic form), acknowledge within 30 days, respond without undue delay and tell the person the outcome. Inserted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 s.103; fully in force 19 June 2026 (note F1, S.I. 2026/82). A failed rights request about an AI system will now usually arrive here first. One unrelated Northern Ireland effect is shown as outstanding.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 19: Notification obligation regarding rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing
items.quote: to each recipient to whom the personal data have been disclosed, unless this proves impossible or involves disproportionate effort
items.why: The duty to pass a correction or erasure down the chain. Where personal data has gone to an AI supplier, a model developer or another recipient, the organisation must tell each of them unless that is impossible or disproportionate, and must tell the person who the recipients are if asked. The existing Article 17 entry refers to this article; it is the legal reason supplier contracts need a route for rights requests. No amendments shown on the page.

items.title: Enforcement Notice: Bristol City Council
items.quote: take 50 months (over 3 years) to complete the SAR backlog
items.why: UK enforcement on the access right, and a UK figure of the kind the brief could not find: a backlog of 170 overdue access requests in March 2023, the oldest from December 2020, rising to 189 by February 2024, which the council itself estimated would take 50 months to clear. The regulator ordered the backlog cleared and processes changed. Limits: one public body, ordinary records and not AI; it shows what the regulator does when requests cannot be met in time. An enforcement notice, not a fine; typed 'regulator guidance' for want of an enforcement type, as with the Serco notice. Dated 27 August 2025 on its face.

items.title: AI how-to sheets: Ensuring and facilitating the exercise of data subjects' rights
items.publisher: Commission Nationale de l'Informatique et des Libertés (CNIL)
items.locator: Sections on rights over training datasets and over AI models; passage beginning 'the CNIL identifies, to date, two main techniques'
items.quote: the most effective is retraining, which makes it possible to erase or rectify data at the heart of the model
items.why: International comparator: the French regulator's practical guidance, more detailed than anything yet published in the UK. Rights apply to training data and to a model unless it is anonymous; developers of generative systems should keep an internal procedure for querying the model to see whether it retained a person's data; retraining is the effective remedy and output filters a second best that leaves the data in place; a request refused today may have to be met as techniques improve. Limits: French guidance under the EU GDPR, not binding in the UK; aimed at developers more than at firms that buy systems. Date is the one shown on the English page.

items.title: 2024 Coordinated Enforcement Action: Implementation of the right of access by controllers
items.locator: Executive summary, p. 2; section 3.1, p. 9; section 4.2.3 'Lack of documented internal procedures', pp. 18-19
items.quote: a lack of a formal documented procedure can heighten the possibility of an infringement of a data subjects rights
items.why: The access-right companion to the erasure report already listed. Thirty regulators across the European Economic Area questioned controllers and 1,185 replied (p. 9). Recurring problems: no documented procedure, requests not recognised when they arrive by an unexpected route, and confusion over how much must be provided. Evidence that readiness fails on process before it fails on technology. Limits: European Economic Area, not the UK; about access generally, not AI; self-reported answers. The address redirects to a path under /system/files/documents/.

items.title: NIST Privacy Framework: A Tool for Improving Privacy through Enterprise Risk Management, Version 1.0
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Appendix A, Table 2, Control-P, 'Data Processing Management (CT.DM-P)', p. 24 (PDF p. 28); p. 17 (PDF p. 21)
items.quote: CT.DM-P4: Data elements can be accessed for deletion.
items.why: A free standard that turns rights readiness into testable system capabilities: each data element can be reached for review (P1), disclosure (P2), alteration (P3) and deletion (P4), and data is destroyed according to policy (P5). Useful as a design checklist for an AI system that holds personal data. Limits: a voluntary United States framework, not UK law; version 1.0 of January 2020 pre-dates generative AI and says nothing about data inside trained models. Whether a later version has been issued was not checked.

items.title: Algorithms that Remember: Model Inversion Attacks and Data Protection Law
items.publisher: arXiv (M. Veale, R. Binns and L. Edwards; Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A 376, 2018)
items.quote: the process of turning training data into machine learned systems is not one-way
items.why: Peer-reviewed work, and an early statement of the argument the regulator now makes: because training data can sometimes be recovered or inferred from a model, a model can itself be personal data, and the rights of access, erasure and objection would then reach it. Explains why the criterion looks beyond the training set. Limits: abstract only read in this pass; written about the EU GDPR in 2018, before large language models; the authors' copy, journal reference as stated on the arXiv page.

items.title: Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models
items.quote: an adversary can perform a training data extraction attack to recover individual training examples by querying the language model
items.why: The experiment behind the concern. By querying a public language model the authors recovered hundreds of passages word for word from its training data, including names, phone numbers and email addresses, some of which appeared in only one training document; larger models were more exposed. If personal data can be pulled out of a model, deleting the training set does not end the organisation's duty. Limits: abstract only read in this pass; one model (GPT-2) and one attack; the authors' preprint, and its conference publication was not checked.
